questions.a: The cutouts are congruent, since turning a figure is allowed

The cutouts are not congruent, since one had to be turned

questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.q: (a) What are congruent figures? (b) Give one example of two congruent objects that you can find in your school bag or classroom.
questions.a: (a) Figures that have the same shape and the same size are congruent; one can be placed exactly over the other. (b) For example, two pages of the same notebook, or two identical erasers from one packet (any pair of exact copies).
s: (a) States same shape and same size, one fits exactly over the other
(b) Gives a correct pair of exact copies

questions.q: True or false: A rectangular card 8 cm by 3 cm lying flat and a rectangular card 3 cm by 8 cm standing on its short side are congruent. Give the reason or the correct statement.
questions.a: True. Both cards have length 8 cm and breadth 3 cm. Turning one card through a quarter turn makes it fit exactly over the other, and turning is allowed when checking congruence.
s: States the verdict: True
Gives the reason: same length and breadth, and a turn makes one fit exactly over the other

questions.q:
Answer briefly.
(a) Raju traces a leaf-shaped cutout. He has to turn the tracing over before it fits exactly on a second cutout. Are the two cutouts congruent?
(b) Two other leaf cutouts look alike, but no small set of measurements is known that fixes the shape of a leaf. How can Raju check whether they are congruent?
(c) Which measurements would you compare to check whether two rectangles are congruent?
questions.a: (a) Yes: a figure may be flipped (turned over) before it is placed on the other, and the tracing then fits exactly. (b) Trace one leaf and place the tracing over the other (superimpose it), rotating or flipping it if needed; if it fits exactly, the leaves are congruent, otherwise not. (c) The two sides: the length and the breadth of each rectangle.
s: (a) Says congruent, as flipping is allowed
(b) Superimposes a tracing, allowing rotating or flipping
(c) Names the length and the breadth

questions.q:
In ΔABC, AB = 5 cm, BC = 6 cm and CA = 7 cm. In ΔPQR, PQ = 5 cm, QR = 6 cm and RP = 7 cm.
(a) Are the triangles congruent? Name the condition.
(b) Write the congruence with the vertices in the correct order.
questions.a: (a) Yes. All three pairs of sides are equal, so they are congruent by the SSS condition. (b) ΔABC ≅ ΔPQR, since AB = PQ, BC = QR and CA = RP.
s: (a) Says congruent by SSS
(b) Writes ΔABC ≅ ΔPQR

questions.q:
Two triangular garden beds are marked with rope. Bed ΔKLM has KL = 3 m, LM = 4 m and MK = 6 m. Bed ΔXYZ has XY = 4 m, YZ = 6 m and ZX = 3 m.
(a) Pair each side of ΔKLM with the equal side of ΔXYZ.
(b) Name the condition and write the congruence with the vertices in order, starting with ΔKLM.
(c) Which angle of ΔXYZ is equal to ∠L?
questions.a: (a) KL = ZX = 3 m, LM = XY = 4 m, MK = YZ = 6 m. (b) SSS; L lies between the 3 m and 4 m sides, and so does X; K lies between the 3 m and 6 m sides, and so does Z. So ΔKLM ≅ ΔZXY. (c) ∠X.
s: (a) Pairs KL-ZX, LM-XY, MK-YZ
(b) Names SSS and writes ΔKLM ≅ ΔZXY
(c) Names ∠X

questions.q:
The triangular frame of a notice board in Asha's school has sides 90 cm, 120 cm and 150 cm. She wants a cardboard copy of exactly the same size and shape.
(a) Is it enough to know the three sides? Name the condition that tells you.
A shop has three cardboard triangles: T1 with sides 120 cm, 150 cm and 90 cm; T2 with sides 90 cm, 120 cm and 160 cm; T3 with sides 150 cm, 90 cm and 120 cm.
(b) Is T1 congruent to the frame? (c) Is T2? (d) Is T3? Give a reason each time.
questions.a: (a) Yes. A triangle with the same three sidelengths is congruent to the frame by the SSS condition, so the angles need not be measured. (b) Yes: T1 has sides 90, 120 and 150 cm, the same as the frame (SSS). (c) No: T2 has a 160 cm side instead of 150 cm, so its sides do not match. (d) Yes: T3 also has sides 90, 120 and 150 cm (SSS).
s: (a) Says the three sides are enough, by SSS
(b) T1 is congruent: same three sides
(c) T2 is not congruent: 160 cm does not match 150 cm
(d) T3 is congruent: same three sides

questions.q:
It is given that ΔRAM ≅ ΔSUN.
I. ∠A = ∠U
II. ΔMRA ≅ ΔNUS is another correct way to write this congruence.
III. RM = SN
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: I and III only
o: I and III only
I and II only
II and III only
I, II and III

questions.q: Joseph draws AB = 7 cm. From A he draws a circle of radius 5 cm and from B a circle of radius 9 cm. The circles cross at E above AB and at F below AB. He says: 'I get two triangles, ΔABE and ΔABF, so three sides do not fix one triangle and SSS fails.' Check his claim.
questions.a: In ΔABE and ΔABF: AE = AF = 5 cm (radius of the first circle), BE = BF = 9 cm (radius of the second circle), and AB is common. So by SSS, ΔABE ≅ ΔABF: the two triangles are the same triangle, one flipped over AB. Joseph's claim is wrong; either triangle is an exact copy, so SSS does not fail.
s: Lists AE = AF = 5 cm, BE = BF = 9 cm and the common side AB
Concludes ΔABE ≅ ΔABF by SSS (one is the other flipped over AB)
Gives the verdict: the claim is wrong, SSS still fixes the triangle

questions.q:
A model bridge uses a triangular panel ΔABC with AB = 6 cm, BC = 8 cm and CA = 9 cm. A spare panel ΔPQR has PQ = 9 cm, QR = 6 cm and RP = 8 cm, and its angle at R measures about 79°.
(a) Is the spare panel congruent to ΔABC? Name the condition.
(b) Write the congruence, starting with ΔABC, with the vertices in the correct order.
(c) Which angle of ΔABC measures about 79°?
(d) Another panel ΔXYZ has sides 6 cm, 8 cm and 10 cm. Can it replace ΔABC? Give a reason.
(e) When the spare panel is fixed in place of ΔABC, at which corner of ΔABC must corner P go?
questions.a: (a) Yes: the sides of ΔPQR are 9, 6 and 8 cm, the same as 6, 8 and 9 cm, so they are congruent by SSS. (b) AB = QR = 6, BC = RP = 8, CA = PQ = 9. B lies between the 6 and 8 cm sides, as R does; A between the 6 and 9 cm sides, as Q does; C between the 8 and 9 cm sides, as P does. So ΔABC ≅ ΔQRP. (c) ∠B, since B corresponds to R. (d) No: 10 cm does not equal 9 cm, so the sides do not match and it is not congruent. (e) At C, since P corresponds to C.
s: (a) Matches the three sides and names SSS
(b) Writes ΔABC ≅ ΔQRP
(c) Names ∠B as about 79°
(d) Rejects ΔXYZ because 10 cm is not 9 cm
(e) Places P at corner C

Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.

questions.q:
(a) State the SAS condition for congruence of two triangles.
(b) In ΔXYZ and ΔLMN, XY = LM and XZ = LN. Which one more pair of equal parts makes them congruent by SAS?
questions.a: (a) If two sides and the angle included between them in one triangle are equal to two sides and the included angle in another triangle, the triangles are congruent. (b) ∠X = ∠L, the angles between the given sides.
s: (a) States SAS with the included angle
(b) Names ∠X = ∠L

questions.q: True or false: Two triangles that each have angles of 40°, 60° and 80° must be congruent. Give the reason or the correct statement.
questions.a: False. Equal angles give the same shape but not always the same size: a small triangle and a much bigger triangle can both have angles 40°, 60° and 80°. So equal angles alone (AAA) do not guarantee congruence.
s: States the verdict: False
Explains that the triangles have the same shape but can differ in size, so AAA is not enough

questions.q: Kiran sends a workshop the data PQ = 8 cm, QR = 5 cm and ∠P = 35° for a triangular plate PQR. The workshop replies that it could cut two different plates from this data. Why?
questions.a: The 35° angle is not between the two given sides, so an arc of 5 cm from Q can cut the line from P at two points
o: The 35° angle is not between the two given sides, so an arc of 5 cm from Q can cut the line from P at two points
Two sides and one angle are never enough to fix any triangle, whichever angle is given to the workshop
The three angles are not all given, so the size of the plate cannot be fixed by the workshop
Sides of 8 cm and 5 cm cannot make a triangle that has an angle of 35° at the corner P

questions.q: Neel has two triangular shelves; each has sides of 30 cm and 40 cm with a 90° angle between those two sides. Tina has two triangular shelves; each has sides of 30 cm and 40 cm and a 35° angle opposite the 30 cm side. Neel says: 'Both my pair and Tina's pair are surely congruent.' How far is he right?
questions.a: Neel is partly right. His own pair has two sides and the included angle equal, so it is congruent by SAS. In Tina's pair the 35° angle is not between the 30 cm and 40 cm sides; that is SSA, which does not guarantee congruence (two different triangles can have these measurements). So her shelves are not surely congruent.
s: Neel's pair: two sides and the included 90° angle, congruent by SAS
Tina's pair: the angle is not included, so it is SSA, which does not guarantee congruence
Verdict: partly right

questions.q:
Ravi, a carpenter in Nagpur, makes triangular corner shelves from plywood. A customer sends three messages, each describing a shelf ΔABC that Ravi must copy exactly.
Message 1: AB = 45 cm, AC = 28 cm and ∠A = 70°.
Message 2: ∠A = 60°, ∠B = 60° and ∠C = 60°.
Message 3: AB = 40 cm, BC = 25 cm and ∠A = 30°.
(a) In Message 1, is the given angle included between the two given sides? How do you know?
(b) Which condition shows that every shelf made from Message 1 will be congruent to the customer's shelf?
(c) Why can Message 2 lead to shelves of different sizes?
(d) Ravi says Message 3 is enough to cut the shelf. Is he right? Justify.
questions.a: (a) Yes: AB and AC both meet at A, so ∠A lies between them. (b) SAS: two sides and the included angle are fixed. (c) Message 2 gives only angles; equal angles fix the shape but not the size, so a small and a large shelf both fit it. (d) No. ∠A is not between AB and BC, so this is SSA. Drawing AB = 40 cm and a line from A at 30°, an arc of 25 cm from B can cut that line at two points, giving two different shelves.
s: (a) Says ∠A is included, as A is the common end of AB and AC
(b) Names the SAS condition
(c) Explains that angles alone fix shape, not size
(d) Says no: SSA, the arc from B can meet the line at two points

questions.q:
A school store has three A-shaped folding ladders. Each ladder has two legs hinged at the top T, with the feet A and B resting on level ground, so that T, A and B form a triangle.
Ladder 1: TA = TB = 2 m and ∠ATB = 40°; its feet are measured to be 1.37 m apart.
Ladder 2: TA = TB = 2 m and ∠ATB = 40°.
Ladder 3: TA = TB = 2 m and its feet are tied by a rope with AB = 1.4 m.
(a) Which condition shows that triangle TAB of Ladder 2 is congruent to that of Ladder 1?
(b) Without measuring, how far apart are the feet of Ladder 2? Give the reason.
(c) Is triangle TAB of Ladder 3 congruent to that of Ladder 1? Give the reason.
(d) Is the angle at T the same in Ladder 3 as in Ladder 1? Explain.
(e) The storekeeper says: 'All the ladders have 2 m legs, so they all stand with the same spread.' Explain what is missing from his reasoning.
questions.a: (a) SAS: TA, TB and the included angle ∠ATB = 40° are equal. (b) 1.37 m, because AB of Ladder 2 corresponds to AB of Ladder 1 in congruent triangles. (c) No: its sides are 2 m, 2 m and 1.4 m, while Ladder 1 has 2 m, 2 m and 1.37 m; the third sides differ, so the sides do not all match. (d) No. If the angles at T were equal, the two triangles would be congruent by SAS and their feet would be equally far apart; but 1.4 m is not 1.37 m, so the angle at T in Ladder 3 is not 40°. (e) Two equal sides alone do not fix a triangle; the angle between the legs (or the third side) must also be equal, so the spread depends on how far the legs are opened.
s: (a) Names SAS with TA, TB and the included 40° angle
(b) Gives 1.37 m as corresponding sides of congruent triangles
(c) Says not congruent, since 1.4 m is not 1.37 m
(d) Argues that an equal angle at T would force equal spreads by SAS, so the angle differs
(e) Says the included angle (or the third side) is missing

questions.q: In ΔABC, ∠A = 45° and ∠B = 65°. What is ∠C?
Two angles and the side between them in one triangle are equal to two angles and the side between them in another triangle. Which condition makes the triangles congruent?
questions.a: ASA (Angle Side Angle)
o: ASA (Angle Side Angle)
SAS (Side Angle Side)
SSA (Side Side Angle)
SSS (Side Side Side)

questions.q:
In ΔABC and ΔXYZ, BC = YZ = 6 cm, ∠B = ∠Y = 45° and ∠C = ∠Z = 65°.
(a) Is the given side included between the two given angles? Say how you know.
(b) Name the condition and write the congruence.
questions.a: (a) Yes: BC joins the vertices B and C, so it lies between ∠B and ∠C (and YZ lies between ∠Y and ∠Z). (b) ASA, so ΔABC ≅ ΔXYZ.
s: (a) Says yes, BC joins the two vertices B and C
(b) Names ASA and writes ΔABC ≅ ΔXYZ

questions.q:
In ΔPQR, ∠P = 40°, ∠Q = 85° and QR = 7 cm. In ΔDEF, ∠D = 40°, ∠E = 85° and EF = 7 cm.
(a) Find ∠R and ∠F.
(b) Using ∠Q, QR and ∠R, which condition shows that the triangles are congruent?
(c) What is the name of the condition for the data as it was first given (two angles and a side not between them)?
questions.a: (a) ∠R = 180° - 40° - 85° = 55°, and likewise ∠F = 55°. (b) ASA: ∠Q = ∠E, QR = EF and ∠R = ∠F, so ΔPQR ≅ ΔDEF. (c) AAS (Angle Angle Side).
s: (a) Finds ∠R = ∠F = 55° using the angle sum
(b) Names ASA with ∠Q, QR, ∠R
(c) Names AAS

Reason (R): When two angles of a triangle are known, the third angle is also fixed by the angle sum.
questions.a: A is false but R is true.
o: A is false but R is true.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.

questions.q:
In ΔKLM, ∠K = 62°, ∠L = 48° and LM = 9 cm. In ΔRST, ∠S = 48°, ∠T = 70° and ST = 9 cm.
(a) Find ∠M and ∠R.
(b) Are the triangles congruent? Name the condition and write the congruence.
questions.a: (a) ∠M = 180° - 62° - 48° = 70°; ∠R = 180° - 48° - 70° = 62°. (b) Yes. ∠L = ∠S = 48°, LM = ST = 9 cm and ∠M = ∠T = 70°, with the side between the angles, so by ASA, ΔKLM ≅ ΔRST.
s: (a) Finds ∠M = 70° and ∠R = 62°
(b) Uses ∠L, LM, ∠M with ∠S, ST, ∠T to give ASA and ΔKLM ≅ ΔRST

questions.q:
For a new school window, a glazier's helpers cut triangular glass panes that must be congruent to a master pane ΔABC with ∠A = 40°, ∠B = 70° and AB = 30 cm. Three helpers report their panes.
Pane P: two angles of 40° and 70°, with a 30 cm side between them.
Pane Q: ΔXYZ with ∠X = 40°, ∠Z = 70° and YZ = 30 cm.
Pane R: ΔKLM with ∠K = 70°, ∠M = 40° and KM = 30 cm.
(a) Find ∠C of the master pane.
(b) Is Pane P congruent to the master pane? Name the condition.
(c) In Pane Q, which angle is opposite the 30 cm side? Is Pane Q congruent to the master? Give a reason.
(d) Decide which panes should be kept. Justify your decision for Pane R.
questions.a: (a) ∠C = 180° - 40° - 70° = 70°. (b) Yes, by ASA: 40°, 30 cm, 70° with the side between the angles, as in the master (∠A, AB, ∠B). (c) The 30 cm side YZ is opposite ∠X = 40° (and ∠Y = 70°). In the master the side opposite the 40° angle is BC, not one of the 30 cm sides (AB is opposite ∠C = 70°), so the 30 cm side of Q is in the wrong position and Q is not congruent. (d) Keep P and R, reject Q. In Pane R, KM lies between ∠K = 70° and ∠M = 40°, just as AB lies between ∠B = 70° and ∠A = 40°, so by ASA ΔABC ≅ ΔMKL.
s: (a) Finds ∠C = 70°
(b) Pane P is congruent by ASA
(c) Pane Q: 30 cm side is opposite 40°, not matching the master, so not congruent
(d) Keeps P and R; R is congruent by ASA with ∠M = ∠A, KM = AB, ∠K = ∠B

questions.q:
ΔABC has ∠A = 55°, ∠B = 65° and AC = 10 cm. Three other triangles are measured.
T1: ΔDEF with ∠D = 55°, ∠E = 65° and DF = 10 cm.
T2: ΔKLM with ∠K = 60°, ∠L = 55° and KL = 10 cm.
T3: ΔXYZ with ∠X = 55°, ∠Y = 65° and XY = 10 cm.
(a) Find ∠C.
(b) Is T1 congruent to ΔABC? Name the condition.
(c) Find ∠M in T2. Is T2 congruent to ΔABC? If so, write the congruence starting with ΔABC.
(d) Is T3 congruent to ΔABC? Give a reason.
(e) What do (b), (c) and (d) show about where the equal side must lie?
questions.a: (a) ∠C = 180° - 55° - 65° = 60°. (b) Yes. ∠A = ∠D, ∠B = ∠E, and AC = DF is the side opposite the 65° angle in both, so they are congruent by AAS (ΔABC ≅ ΔDEF). (c) ∠M = 180° - 60° - 55° = 65°. KL lies between ∠K = 60° and ∠L = 55°, as AC lies between ∠C = 60° and ∠A = 55°, so by ASA, ΔABC ≅ ΔLMK. (d) No. XY is opposite ∠Z = 60°, but the 10 cm side of ΔABC (AC) is opposite the 65° angle, so the equal sides are not corresponding sides. (e) The equal sides must be corresponding sides, lying in the same position relative to the equal angles (opposite equal angles); equal angles with a side placed differently do not give congruence.
s: (a) Finds ∠C = 60°
(b) T1 congruent by AAS
(c) Finds ∠M = 65° and writes ΔABC ≅ ΔLMK by ASA
(d) T3 not congruent: the 10 cm side is opposite 60°, not 65°
(e) States that the equal side must be in the corresponding position

II. The RHS condition is used only for right-angled triangles.
III. Two sides and any one angle (SSA) always guarantee congruence.
Which of the statements are correct?

o: I and II only
II and III only
I only

questions.q:
ΔABC has ∠B = 90°, AC = 10 cm and BC = 6 cm. ΔXYZ has ∠Y = 90°, XZ = 10 cm and YZ = 6 cm.
(a) Name the hypotenuse of each triangle.
(b) Name the condition and write the congruence.
questions.a: (a) AC in ΔABC and XZ in ΔXYZ, as they are opposite the right angles. (b) RHS: right angles ∠B = ∠Y, hypotenuses AC = XZ and sides BC = YZ, so ΔABC ≅ ΔXYZ.
s: (a) Names AC and XZ as the hypotenuses
(b) Names RHS and writes ΔABC ≅ ΔXYZ

questions.q:
Answer each part.
(a) What is the hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle?
(b) State the RHS condition.
(c) List the five conditions that guarantee that two triangles are congruent.
(d) ΔPQR has ∠Q = 90°, PR = 11 cm and QR = 6 cm. ΔLMN has ∠M = 90°, LN = 11 cm and MN = 6 cm. Are they congruent? Write the congruence.
(e) In (d), which angle of ΔLMN is equal to ∠P?
questions.a: (a) The side opposite the right angle. (b) If two right-angled triangles have equal hypotenuses and one other pair of equal sides, they are congruent. (c) SSS, SAS, ASA, AAS and RHS. (d) Yes, by RHS: ∠Q = ∠M = 90°, PR = LN = 11 cm, QR = MN = 6 cm, so ΔPQR ≅ ΔLMN. (e) ∠L.
s: (a) Side opposite the right angle
(b) States RHS: right angle, hypotenuse and one side equal
(c) Lists SSS, SAS, ASA, AAS, RHS
(d) Says congruent by RHS, ΔPQR ≅ ΔLMN
(e) Names ∠L

questions.q: Two right-angled roof trusses are cut for a model house. Truss 1 has a hypotenuse of 15 cm and another side of 9 cm. On truss 2, the two sides that form the right angle are 9 cm and 15 cm. Aman says RHS makes them congruent. Which response is correct?
questions.a: No: in truss 2 the 15 cm side is not the hypotenuse, so the parts do not correspond
o: No: in truss 2 the 15 cm side is not the hypotenuse, so the parts do not correspond
Yes: both have a right angle and sides of 9 cm and 15 cm, which is all RHS needs
Yes, by SAS: in both, two sides of 9 cm and 15 cm and a right angle are equal
No: two right-angled triangles can never be shown congruent from two sides alone

questions.q: Using the RHS construction, show that there is no right-angled triangle PQR with ∠Q = 90°, QR = 5 cm and hypotenuse PR = 4 cm.
questions.a: Draw QR = 5 cm and a line l perpendicular to QR at Q; P must lie on l with PR = 4 cm, so cut an arc of radius 4 cm from R. The arc cuts QR at a point 1 cm short of Q (5 - 4 = 1), and when it is drawn it stays on R's side of l and never reaches l. So there is no point P, and no such triangle can be drawn.
s: Draws QR = 5 cm and the perpendicular line l at Q, with P to be found on l
Cuts the 4 cm arc from R and notes that it stops 1 cm short of Q and does not reach l
Concludes that P cannot be marked, so the triangle is impossible

questions.q:
A mason in a temple courtyard needs right-angled stone tiles congruent to a master tile ΔDEF with ∠E = 90°, DF = 17 cm and DE = 8 cm. Three tiles are checked.
Tile 1: ΔKLM with ∠L = 90°, KM = 17 cm and KL = 8 cm.
Tile 2: ΔUVW with ∠V = 90°, UV = 8 cm and VW = 17 cm.
Tile 3: ΔRST with ∠S = 90°, RT = 17 cm and ST = 8 cm.
(a) Name the hypotenuse of the master tile. (b) Is Tile 1 congruent to it? (c) Is Tile 2? (d) Is Tile 3? Where congruent, write the congruence starting with ΔDEF.
questions.a: (a) DF, the side opposite the right angle ∠E. (b) Yes, by RHS: ∠E = ∠L, DF = KM = 17 cm, DE = KL = 8 cm, so ΔDEF ≅ ΔKLM. (c) No: in Tile 2 the 17 cm side VW forms the right angle with UV, so it is not the hypotenuse; its hypotenuse UW is a different, longer side, so the parts do not match. (d) Yes, by RHS: ∠E = ∠S, DF = TR = 17 cm, DE = TS = 8 cm. D matches T, E matches S and F matches R, so ΔDEF ≅ ΔTSR.
s: (a) Names DF as the hypotenuse
(b) Tile 1 congruent by RHS, ΔDEF ≅ ΔKLM
(c) Tile 2 not congruent: 17 cm is not its hypotenuse
(d) Tile 3 congruent by RHS, ΔDEF ≅ ΔTSR

questions.q: ΔABC has ∠B = 90°, ∠A = 50° and AB = 8 cm. ΔDEF has ∠E = 90°, ∠D = 50° and DE = 8 cm. Sana says: 'They are right-angled triangles, but no hypotenuse is given, so RHS cannot be used and the triangles cannot be shown congruent.' (a) Is she right that RHS cannot be used here? (b) Which other condition applies, using the parts at A and B? (c) Find ∠C and ∠F. (d) Give your verdict on Sana's claim and write the congruence.
questions.a: (a) Yes, RHS needs the hypotenuses (AC and DF) to be equal, and they are not given. (b) ASA: ∠A = ∠D = 50°, AB = DE = 8 cm (the side between them) and ∠B = ∠E = 90°. (c) ∠C = ∠F = 180° - 90° - 50° = 40°. (d) Her claim is wrong: RHS is only one of five conditions, and ASA shows ΔABC ≅ ΔDEF.
s: (a) Agrees RHS cannot be used, since the hypotenuses are not given
(b) Identifies ASA with ∠A, AB, ∠B
(c) Finds ∠C = ∠F = 40°
(d) Rejects the claim and writes ΔABC ≅ ΔDEF

questions.q: In ΔABC, AB = AC and ∠B = 65°. What is ∠C?
What is the measure of each angle of an equilateral triangle?

In ΔPQR, PQ = PR and ∠P = 70°.
(a) Which two angles are equal, and why?
(b) Find each of them.
questions.a: (a) ∠Q = ∠R, because they are opposite the equal sides PR and PQ. (b) ∠Q + ∠R = 180° - 70° = 110°, so ∠Q = ∠R = 55°.
s: (a) Names ∠Q = ∠R as angles opposite equal sides
(b) Finds ∠Q = ∠R = 55°

questions.q: True or false: In ΔXYZ, if XY = YZ, then ∠X = ∠Z. Give the reason or the correct statement.
questions.a: True. The side XY is opposite ∠Z and the side YZ is opposite ∠X. Angles opposite equal sides are equal, so ∠X = ∠Z.
s: States the verdict: True
Explains that XY is opposite ∠Z and YZ is opposite ∠X, and angles opposite equal sides are equal

questions.q:
In an isosceles triangle the angle between the two equal sides is 36°.
(a) What is the sum of the other two angles?
(b) Find each of the other two angles.
(c) Is the 36° angle the largest angle of this triangle? Give a reason.
questions.a: (a) 180° - 36° = 144°. (b) The other two angles are opposite the equal sides, so they are equal: 144° ÷ 2 = 72° each. (c) No: 72° is larger than 36°, so the two base angles are the largest.
s: (a) Finds the sum 144°
(b) Finds each base angle as 72°
(c) Says no, since 72° is more than 36°

questions.q:
Road-safety boards near a school in Guntur are cut from metal sheets. The 'give way' board ABC is an equilateral triangle with each side 60 cm. A second board PQR is an isosceles triangle with PQ = PR = 50 cm and ∠P = 40°. The welder fixes a support bracket at the corner of each board that has the largest angle.
(a) What is each angle of board ABC?
(b) Which two angles of board PQR are equal, and why?
(c) Find ∠Q of board PQR.
(d) At which corner or corners of each board can the welder fix the bracket? Explain.
questions.a: (a) 60°, since all three angles of an equilateral triangle are equal and add up to 180°. (b) ∠Q = ∠R, because they are opposite the equal sides PR and PQ. (c) ∠Q = (180° - 40°) ÷ 2 = 70°. (d) On board ABC every corner has 60°, so any corner will do. On board PQR the largest angle is 70° at Q and at R (more than 40° at P), so the bracket goes at Q or R, not at P.
s: (a) Gives 60° for each angle of ABC
(b) Names ∠Q = ∠R as opposite equal sides
(c) Finds ∠Q = 70°
(d) Any corner of ABC; Q or R of PQR

questions.q:
Assertion (A): In ΔPQR with PQ = PR, if ∠P = 50°, then ∠Q = 50°.
Reason (R): In a triangle, angles opposite equal sides are equal.
questions.a: A is false but R is true.
o: A is false but R is true.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.

questions.q:
(a) ΔPQR has PQ = PR and ∠Q = 38°. Find ∠P.
(b) ΔXYZ has XY = XZ and ∠X = 38°. Find ∠Y.
s: (a) Uses ∠R = 38° and finds ∠P = 104°
(b) Treats 38° as the apex angle and finds ∠Y = 71°

questions.q:
ΔABC is equilateral. A point D lies inside it so that DB = DC and ∠BDC = 100°. The segments DB, DC and AD are joined.
(a) What is each angle of ΔABC?
(b) Find ∠DBC and ∠DCB.
(c) Find ∠ABD.
(d) Show that ΔABD ≅ ΔACD and name the condition.
(e) Find ∠BAD and ∠ADB.
questions.a: (a) 60° each. (b) ∠DBC = ∠DCB, opposite the equal sides DC and DB, so each is (180° - 100°) ÷ 2 = 40°. (c) ∠ABD = ∠ABC - ∠DBC = 60° - 40° = 20°. (d) AB = AC (sides of the equilateral triangle), DB = DC (given) and AD is common, so ΔABD ≅ ΔACD by SSS. (e) From (d), ∠BAD = ∠CAD, so ∠BAD = 60° ÷ 2 = 30°. Then ∠ADB = 180° - 20° - 30° = 130°.
s: (a) Gives 60° for each angle of ΔABC
(b) Finds ∠DBC = ∠DCB = 40°
(c) Finds ∠ABD = 20°
(d) Proves ΔABD ≅ ΔACD by SSS using AB = AC, DB = DC and the common AD
(e) Finds ∠BAD = 30° and ∠ADB = 130°

questions.q: ABCD is a square tile with its corners in the order A, B, C, D, and both diagonals AC and BD are drawn. Ritu wants to prove ΔABD ≅ ΔBAC using only what she knows about a square. Which reasoning works?
questions.a: SAS: AD = BC, ∠DAB = ∠CBA = 90°, and AB is common
o: SAS: AD = BC, ∠DAB = ∠CBA = 90°, and AB is common
ASA: ∠DAB = ∠CBA = 90°, and AB is common
SSS: all four sides of the square are equal
RHS: the right angles and the hypotenuses BD and AC

questions.q:
In ΔABC, AB = AC. The side BA is extended beyond A to a point D, and the side CA is extended beyond A to a point E, with AD = AE. BE and CD are joined.
I. ΔABE ≅ ΔACD by the SAS condition, using ∠BAE = ∠CAD as vertically opposite angles
II. BE = CD
III. ΔABE ≅ ΔADC
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: I and II only
o: I and II only
I only
II and III only
I, II and III

questions.q:
ΔPQS and ΔRQS lie on opposite sides of their common side QS, with ∠PQS = ∠RQS and ∠PSQ = ∠RSQ.
(a) Which condition shows that ΔPQS ≅ ΔRQS? Name the three equal parts.
(b) What follows for the sides PQ and RQ?
questions.a: (a) ASA: ∠PQS = ∠RQS, the common side QS, and ∠PSQ = ∠RSQ, with QS between the two angles. (b) PQ = RQ, since they are corresponding sides of the congruent triangles.
s: (a) Names ASA with the two pairs of angles and the common side QS
(b) Concludes PQ = RQ as corresponding sides

questions.q: ΔABC and ΔDCB stand on the same base BC, on the same side of it, with AB = DC and ∠ABC = ∠DCB. Show that AC = DB.
questions.a: In ΔABC and ΔDCB: AB = DC (given), ∠ABC = ∠DCB (given), and BC = CB (common side). The angles lie between the given sides, so ΔABC ≅ ΔDCB by SAS, with A matching D, B matching C and C matching B. Hence AC and DB are corresponding sides, so AC = DB.
s: Lists AB = DC, ∠ABC = ∠DCB and the common side BC
Concludes ΔABC ≅ ΔDCB by SAS with the correct order
Deduces AC = DB as corresponding sides

questions.q: Nikhil says: 'A diagonal always cuts a four-sided figure into two congruent triangles, as it does in a rectangle.' Test his claim with a quadrilateral ABCD (corners in that order) that has AB = 4 cm, BC = 6 cm, CD = 7 cm and DA = 5 cm, cut along the diagonal AC.
questions.a: The diagonal AC makes ΔABC with sides 4 cm, 6 cm and AC, and ΔADC with sides 5 cm, 7 cm and AC. Apart from the common side AC, the sides 4 and 6 cm cannot be matched with 5 and 7 cm, so the triangles do not have the same sidelengths and are not congruent. Nikhil's claim is wrong: it works in a rectangle (and a square) because opposite sides are equal, not in every four-sided figure.
s: Lists the sides of ΔABC (4, 6, AC) and ΔADC (5, 7, AC)
Shows the sides cannot match, so the triangles are not congruent
Concludes the claim is false in general and explains why the rectangle is special

questions.q: In ΔABC, AB = AC. Points D and E lie on BC with BD = CE, and AD and AE are joined. Which conclusion is correct?
questions.a: AD = AE, because ΔABD ≅ ΔACE by SAS, using ∠B = ∠C
o: AD = AE, because ΔABD ≅ ΔACE by SAS, using ∠B = ∠C
AD = AE, because ΔABD ≅ ΔACE by SSS, using AB = AC
AD = AE cannot be shown, because no pair of angles is given equal
AD = DE, because ΔABD ≅ ΔADE by SAS, using AD as common

questions.q:
In a school garden in Nagpur, two straight hedges meet at a corner O. A straight path OC runs between them, making an angle of 35° with each hedge. A water tap T is fixed on the path, 10 m from O. Pipes run from T to points P and Q on the two hedges, each pipe at right angles to its hedge. The gardener measures TP = 5.7 m and OP = 8.2 m. Pipe costs ₹90 per metre.
(a) Find ∠OTP and ∠OTQ.
(b) Which condition shows ΔOPT ≅ ΔOQT? Write the three equal parts.
(c) Find TQ and OQ without measuring them, giving the reason.
(d) The gardener has ₹1,000 to buy both pipes TP and TQ. Is it enough? Decide and show your working.
questions.a: (a) In ΔOPT, ∠OTP = 180° - 90° - 35° = 55°; in ΔOQT, ∠OTQ = 180° - 90° - 35° = 55°. (b) AAS: ∠POT = ∠QOT = 35°, ∠OPT = ∠OQT = 90°, and the side OT (10 m) is common, so ΔOPT ≅ ΔOQT. (c) TQ and OQ correspond to TP and OP, so TQ = TP = 5.7 m and OQ = OP = 8.2 m. (d) Total pipe = 5.7 + 5.7 = 11.4 m, costing 11.4 × 90 = ₹1,026. This is more than ₹1,000, so the money is not enough (₹26 short).
s: (a) Finds both angles as 55°
(b) Names AAS with the two angle pairs and the common side OT
(c) TQ = 5.7 m and OQ = 8.2 m as corresponding sides
(d) Finds ₹1,026 and decides ₹1,000 is not enough

questions.q:
ABCD is a rectangle with its corners in the order A, B, C, D, AB = 16 cm and AD = 6 cm. M is the midpoint of AB, and MD and MC are joined. ∠AMD is measured as 37°.
(a) Find AM and MB.
(b) Which condition shows ΔMAD ≅ ΔMBC? Write the three equal parts.
(c) What follows for MD and MC, and for ∠AMD and ∠BMC?
(d) Find ∠BMC and ∠DMC.
(e) Find ∠MDC and ∠MCD, saying why they are equal.
questions.a: (a) AM = MB = 16 ÷ 2 = 8 cm. (b) SAS: AM = BM = 8 cm, ∠MAD = ∠MBC = 90° (angles of a rectangle), AD = BC = 6 cm (opposite sides of a rectangle), with each right angle between the two sides. So ΔMAD ≅ ΔMBC. (c) MD = MC and ∠AMD = ∠BMC, as corresponding parts. (d) ∠BMC = ∠AMD = 37°; AMB is a straight line, so ∠DMC = 180° - 37° - 37° = 106°. (e) In ΔMDC, MD = MC, so the angles opposite these sides are equal: ∠MCD = ∠MDC. Each = (180° - 106°) ÷ 2 = 37°.
s: (a) AM = MB = 8 cm
(b) Proves ΔMAD ≅ ΔMBC by SAS with the three parts
(c) MD = MC and ∠AMD = ∠BMC
(d) ∠BMC = 37° and ∠DMC = 106°
(e) ∠MDC = ∠MCD = 37°, as angles opposite equal sides
